Earlier this year, Apple raised prices sharply in response to the ongoing global memory crisis. For example, the iPad Air jumped from US$599 to US$749; the M5 MacBook Pro went from US$1,699 to US$1,999; and the Apple TV climbed from US$129 to US$199. These are just a few examples — the point is that the increases are quite steep.

It makes you wonder whether Apple will roll out major upgrades to justify these new price tags.

Of course, some Apple products are about to receive significant updates, and the MacBook Pro and iPad mini are two of them. As for products that won't see major changes anytime soon, I really can't imagine Apple successfully selling older designs at higher prices and convincing consumers they're getting their money's worth — especially given the current secondhand market.

If you could pick up an M4 iPad Air for US$599 (or even as low as US$499) just a few months ago, why would you pay US$749 for one now? The higher the price, the more glaring this contradiction becomes.

Several Apple products have barely changed in years. The iPad Air has used the same design and feature set since 2020, with only chip upgrades and Apple Pencil Pro support added along the way. The basic iPad has largely remained the same since 2022, and the iMac hasn't seen any notable changes since 2021.

Do these products absolutely need a redesign? Not necessarily. But I think Apple could take some steps to make them more appealing at these prices — for instance, giving the iMac a miniLED display, offering a 120Hz refresh rate on the iPad Air, or moving to a fully laminated display on the entry-level iPad.

Compared with the size of the price hikes, the cost of these upgrades would be relatively small, yet they could help consumers accept the new pricing. That said, Apple could also consider trimming specs on certain products to offset the price pressure — for example, bringing back a 128GB option for the iPhone.

What do you make of where Apple's product lineup sits after these price increases? Share your thoughts in the comments.
